title: End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers
authors: Nicolas Carion, Francisco Massa, Gabriel Synnaeve, Nicolas Usunier, Alexander Kirillov, Sergey Zagoruyko

blocks.html: Classic object detectors are full of hand-designed machinery: anchor boxes, region proposals, and a non-maximum suppression (NMS) step to remove duplicate detections of the same object. DETR (DEtection TRansformer) throws all of that out and treats detection as a single problem: directly predict the set of objects in an image, in one shot.

It does this with two ingredients. First, a set-based global loss that forces unique predictions through bipartite matching, so each ground-truth object is matched to exactly one prediction — no duplicates, no NMS needed. Second, a Transformer encoder-decoder that reasons about all objects and the whole image at once using attention.
DETR ... views object detection as a direct set prediction problem ... removing the need for many hand-designed components like a non-maximum suppression procedure or anchor generation.

The result is a genuinely end-to-end detector that, despite its simplicity, matches a well-tuned Faster R-CNN on COCO — around 42 AP — and extends cleanly to panoptic segmentation. Its main weakness is on small objects, which later work addressed.

Detectors like Faster R-CNN do not predict objects directly. They generate a large number of candidate boxes (from anchors or proposals), classify and refine each one, and then run NMS to collapse the many near-duplicate boxes that inevitably cover the same object. These steps carry assumptions and hyperparameters — anchor scales, IoU thresholds, NMS thresholds — that must be tuned and that leak prior knowledge into the model.

DETR's goal is to make the pipeline end-to-end, the way machine translation became end-to-end with sequence models. If the network can directly output a small set of final predictions and be trained with a loss that scores that set as a whole, all the surrogate steps disappear.

The hard part is that a set has no natural order, and the model must avoid emitting two predictions for one object. A naive loss that pairs prediction $i$ with ground truth $i$ would be meaningless. DETR solves this with bipartite matching, described next.

pages.title: Set prediction loss
pages.subtitle: Bipartite matching with the Hungarian algorithm

blocks.html: DETR always outputs a fixed number $N$ of predictions (e.g. 100), more than the objects in any image. To train it, we first find the best one-to-one assignment between the $N$ predictions and the ground-truth objects (the ground truth is padded with 'no object' tokens to size $N$). We search over permutations $\sigma$ for the one that minimizes the total matching cost:

Reading this: $y_i$ is the $i$-th ground-truth object, $\hat{y}_{\sigma(i)}$ is the prediction assigned to it under permutation $\sigma$, and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{match}}$ scores how well a prediction's class and box fit that object. The optimal assignment $\hat{\sigma}$ is found efficiently with the Hungarian algorithm. This one-to-one matching is exactly what removes duplicates: each object claims a single prediction.

Once matched, the network is trained with a loss combining classification (negative log-likelihood of the correct class) and box regression. The box term blends an L1 loss with a generalized IoU term so it works regardless of box scale:
In words: penalize both the geometric overlap error (IoU) and the raw coordinate error (L1), each weighted by a $\lambda$. Using IoU alongside L1 keeps large and small boxes on comparable footing.

pages.title: The DETR architecture
pages.subtitle: CNN backbone, Transformer, and object queries

blocks.html: The model has three parts. A CNN backbone (e.g. ResNet-50) turns the image into a grid of feature vectors. These are flattened, augmented with positional encodings, and fed to a Transformer encoder, whose self-attention lets every image location attend to every other — giving global context that is hard to get with convolutions alone.

The Transformer decoder is where detection happens. It takes a fixed set of $N$ learned embeddings called object queries. Each query is a slot that attends to the encoded image and to the other queries, and is then decoded into one prediction: a class label (possibly 'no object') and a bounding box. Because queries attend to each other, they coordinate to cover different objects — the model learns not to fire twice on the same thing.

items: Backbone: image → feature map (lower resolution, many channels).
Encoder: self-attention over all spatial positions for global reasoning.
Decoder: N object queries attend to image features and each other, in parallel.
Heads: a shared feed-forward network turns each decoded query into (class, box).

blocks.html: Unlike autoregressive Transformers, the decoder runs in parallel — all $N$ objects are predicted at once, not one token at a time. The whole system is differentiable end-to-end, with no anchors and no NMS.

On COCO, DETR is competitive with a strong, well-tuned Faster R-CNN baseline. The ResNet-101 variant (DETR-DC5) reaches roughly 44 AP, and the base ResNet-50 model sits around 42 AP — comparable overall while using a far simpler pipeline.

The pattern is revealing: DETR is notably better on large objects (its global self-attention easily covers big regions) but worse on small objects than the FPN-based Faster R-CNN. The fixed low-resolution feature map and limited number of queries make tiny objects harder — the most-cited limitation of the original model.

DETR extends to panoptic segmentation (labeling both things and stuff at the pixel level) by simply adding a small mask head on top of the trained detector's object queries. Each query that produces a box can also produce a mask, and the unified design is competitive with specialized panoptic methods.

The attention maps are also interpretable: visualizing decoder attention shows each object query focusing on the extremities of its assigned object, and encoder self-attention already separates individual instances. This gives a clear picture of how the model decides, which anchor-based detectors lack.
DETR can be naturally extended to ... panoptic segmentation, by training a small extension on top of a pre-trained DETR.

DETR showed that object detection could be reframed as a clean set-prediction problem solvable end-to-end with a Transformer, deleting decades of hand-engineered components. Even though its accuracy on small objects and its slow convergence left room to improve, it opened a whole research line.

items: Reformulated detection as direct set prediction with a bipartite-matching loss — no NMS, no anchors.
Used a Transformer encoder-decoder with learned object queries to predict all objects in parallel.
Matched Faster R-CNN (~42 AP) on COCO with a much simpler pipeline; extended to panoptic segmentation.
Inspired follow-ups (Deformable DETR, DINO) that fixed small-object accuracy and slow training.
